item.title: The Many Lives of ELIZA
item.dc:creator: Alex Wright
item.description: Source code preserved on fading fanfold paper became the focus of a four-year international collaboration.
item.content:encoded:
“HOW DO YOU DO. PLEASE TELL ME YOUR PROBLEM.”

With those words, ELIZA made its debut in the pages of this magazine in January 1966. Ever since, Joseph Weizenbaum’s creation has served as a kind of Platonic object for generations of computer scientists, evoking the tantalizing possibilities of talking to a machine.

Yet vanishingly few people have ever encountered the “real” ELIZA. Almost every version in circulation is an imitation, descended directly or indirectly from Weizenbaum’s original article. For decades, the source code had all but disappeared. But a recent multiyear research effort has shed new light on the story of ELIZA’s origins, and on its creator’s complex legacy.

This latest effort began in 2021, when researcher Jeff Shrager enlisted the help of MIT archivist Myles Crowley to search through Weizenbaum’s papers. During a remote archival session, Crowley opened a folder labeled “Computer Conversations” containing a long-forgotten printout of ELIZA’s original source code. The 411 lines of MAD-SLIP code, preserved on fading fanfold paper, became the focus of a four-year international collaboration among researchers in computer science, media studies, and the digital humanities.

That research culminated earlier this year in the publication of Inventing ELIZA,a a critical examination of Weizenbaum and his Pygmalion-inspired prodigy. The project also yielded a faithful reconstruction of the original software, including a Web-based simulation of a 1960s teletype and a version running on an emulated IBM 7094 mainframe.

Although widely remembered as a computerized therapist, ELIZA was originally conceived as a more multifaceted conversationalist: an interpreter capable of running different scripts. The famous DOCTOR persona was only one of the roles Weizenbaum had in mind. He also planned to enable ELIZA to converse as a travel agent, a mathematician, a theater critic, a poet, and even a “Regular Joe” character who could make small talk about New England.

“There was no one ELIZA,” said Sarah Ciston, a professor at the Academy of Media Arts in Cologne, Germany, and co-author of the book. Beyond the different scripts, the program spawned countless imitations written in different languages for different platforms—including the now-almost-canonical version that has shipped as part of GNU Emacs since the mid-1980s. None of these later versions, however, used any of Weizenbaum’s source code.

More surprisingly, the original code diverged in critical respects from the program described in the 1966 paper. “The most remarkable finding of all is that the source code does not follow the algorithm in the article,” said David M. Berry, a digital humanist at the U.K.’s University of Sussex and one of the researchers involved in reconstructing the program.

Among other things, Weizenbaum had neglected to mention that ELIZA treated the word “but” as a delimiter, allowing it to break sentences into smaller fragments. The discrepancies suggest ELIZA was still evolving around the time Weizenbaum submitted his paper.

Yet the recovered code offers more than a glimpse into ELIZA’s inner workings. It also reveals something of Weizenbaum himself, whom Mark Marino, a professor of writing at the University of Southern California and another contributor to Inventing ELIZA, describes as a “playwright, inventor, performer, and con artist.”

The original DOCTOR script was as much a theatrical performance as it was a programming feat. By adopting the persona of a Rogerian psychotherapist, ELIZA could create the appearance of a conversation by reflecting users’ own statements back at them, often in the form of carefully worded questions.

Weizenbaum sustained that illusion through a clever combination of pattern matching, text manipulation, and carefully scripted responses that ranged from the solicitous “WHAT DOES THAT SUGGEST TO YOU” to the decidedly less empathetic “I DON’T CARE ABOUT NAMES.” In truth, the technique required relatively little understanding or interpretation of what people were actually saying.

With its clever rhetorical flourishes embedded in a remarkably concise body of code, ELIZA remains a testament to what Berry calls “the creativity of computing and the possibilities of making a lot with not very much.”

Marino describes the phenomenon as a collaboration between the program and the human imagination: “Half a machine and half our brains doing something. Every human conversation requires you to fill in a lot of things about the person you’re talking to. A conversation with a chatbot is an illusion, in the same way that film is an illusion.”

Weizenbaum harbored no such illusions himself. Indeed, he believed that exposing the program’s inner workings would help people understand the limits of computational intelligence.

“Weizenbaum thought that by showing people, hey, there’s no magic here, I will show you how it works,” says Ciston, “and you’ll see that it’s not magic, and then you will not believe the magic anymore. And that’s not what happened at all.”

Instead, ELIZA captured the public imagination, spurred on by articles in Playboy, The Boston Globe, The New York Times, and elsewhere. Talking computers also were becoming a fixture of pop culture, from Star Trek to 2001: A Space Odyssey and countless subsequent science-fiction portrayals of artificial intelligence. Yet even as ELIZA’s popularity elevated Weizenbaum’s reputation—helping him secure tenure at MIT—he started to worry about the possible unintended impacts of his creation.

When Stanford psychiatrist Kenneth Colby, an early collaborator of Weizenbaum’s, published a paper proposing the use of computers for psychiatric treatment, Weizenbaum grew concerned about what he saw as the risks of an uncritical embrace of artificial intelligence.

Those misgivings only deepened with the ongoing escalation of the Vietnam War, as many of his fellow scientists at MIT started to question the military applications of their research. In 1969, Weizenbaum lent his support to an antiwar research stoppage at the university, alongside notable fellow MIT faculty like Noam Chomsky.

In 1976, Weizenbaum published Computer Power and Human Reason: From Judgment to Calculation,b a withering critique of the computer science profession. He warned against allowing computers to make moral or ethical judgments, arguing that it would be a “monstrous obscenity” to suggest that the complex ethical judgments required of a judge—or a psychiatrist—could be reduced to a computational problem. “There are certain tasks which computers ought not be made to do,” he wrote, “independent of whether computers can be made to do them.”

Over the years to come, Weizenbaum became one of the industry’s most visible Cassandras. “I have pronounced heresy and I am a heretic,” he declared in a 1977 interview with The New York Times.

Today, his warnings seem eerily prescient. The material simplicity of ELIZA stands in stark contrast to the vast computational power of today’s large language models. Yet despite these differences, both kinds of systems shed light on a curiously human tendency to attribute powers of understanding to machines well beyond what they actually possess.

Sixty years after ELIZA first asked users to tell it their problems, the questions Weizenbaum raised remain unresolved: What does it mean for a computer to understand us? And how much authority should we entrust to machines that appear to do so?

“We’re interested in the questions about what it means to be human,” said Ciston. “Asking that about machines is more about us being curious about ourselves.”

Further Reading
